classification.difficultyReason: Constructs two configurations and combines square, equilateral and isosceles triangle properties to justify both possible angles.

content.prompt: $ABCD$ is a square and $AEB$ is an equilateral triangle. Calculate the two possible values of the size of $\angle DEC$.

inlines.text: Place the equilateral triangle on each side of AB and use the equal base angles of triangles ADE and BCE.

answer.worked:
Draw square $ABCD$ with vertices in order, then consider the two possible positions of $E$. Join $DE$ and $CE$.

Since $AD=AB=AE$ and $BC=AB=BE$, triangles $ADE$ and $BCE$ are isosceles. Also, $\angle AEB=60^\circ$.

When $E$ is inside the square:
$$\begin{align*}\angle DAE=\angle CBE&=90^\circ-60^\circ\\\angle DAE=\angle CBE&=30^\circ\\\angle AED=\angle BEC&=\frac{180^\circ-30^\circ}{2}\\\angle AED=\angle BEC&=75^\circ\\\angle DEC&=360^\circ-60^\circ-75^\circ-75^\circ\\\angle DEC&=150^\circ\end{align*}$$
The final subtraction uses angles in a revolution at $E$.

When $E$ is on the opposite side of $AB$ from the square:
$$\begin{align*}\angle DAE=\angle CBE&=90^\circ+60^\circ\\\angle DAE=\angle CBE&=150^\circ\\\angle AED=\angle BEC&=\frac{180^\circ-150^\circ}{2}\\\angle AED=\angle BEC&=15^\circ\\\angle DEC&=60^\circ-15^\circ-15^\circ\\\angle DEC&=30^\circ\end{align*}$$
Here $ED$ and $EC$ lie inside $\angle AEB$, so adjacent angles give the final subtraction.
